body:
> `indices` of binary, multiary and kernel function operations went through `construct_regionally(intersect_indices, loc, operands...)`. When an operand is itself an operation with more operands (for example `c * Δz`, where `Δz` is a `KernelFunctionOperation` with arguments `(Center(), Center(), Center())`), inference reaches the same `construct_regionally` call with a longer argument list while the outer one is still on the stack, and widens it to `Vararg{Any}` to guarantee termination. Because `dim` was a keyword argument, constant propagation could not recover the result either, so `indices` was inferred as `Tuple{Any, Any, Any}` and `axes` as `Union{OneTo, UnitRange}`, and `_mapreducedim!` dispatched `getindex` dynamically. This only happened when the inner operation's `indices` was not yet in the inference cache, so the first such expression compiled in a process stayed slow for the rest of the session (issue #6351: `compute!` of a nested lazy `Integral` took 11.3 ms with 156,555 allocations instead of 0.008 ms with 7 allocations).
> 
> Two changes, each needed for a concrete result in all cases:
> 
> * `intersect_indices` intersects all three dimensions at once with `map` over the index and location tuples, folding over the operands. Without a per-dimension `dim` index into heterogeneous tuples, the result type no longer depends on constant propagation. This alone also fixes expressions such as `s + s` with `s = Field(c; indices = (:, :, 2))`, which were inferred as a union of tuples even without any recursion.
> * Single-region operations call `intersect_indices` directly. The tuple-wise rewrite alone still widened when a kernel function operation wraps an operation with more operands than the kernel has arguments (e.g. `K(c * d)` for a single-argument kernel). Operations on multi-region grids keep `construct_regionally` through new `indices` methods in `MultiRegion`, because their operands' indices are `MultiRegionObject`s.

Fix #6351.
title: Make the inferred type of operation indices independent of the inference cache

We talked about this a lot of times, I think we never did it because (1) we did not have these amazing automatic benchmarks in place and (2) it is a tedious refactoring work. (1) was fixed some time ago and (2) is LLM-enabled :)

The idea is simple: divisions are expensive -> most divisions are divisions by grid metrics -> brutally just store the reciprocals of all the metrics in the grid so we never have to divide by grid quantities.

Disclaimer: This will increase parameter space for old GPUs, however, after #6270 we can reduce significantly this parameter memory so there should be no issues.

@glwagner @jackdfranklin

body:
Closes #6329.

`run!(sim::ReactantSimulation)` traced the first time step before the loop for every timestepper. Only `QuasiAdamsBashforth2TimeStepper` needs that, for its forward-Euler first step; `euler` reaches no other stepper (`reactant_model_time_step!`), so for them the peeled step was the loop body exactly and the program carried the step body twice.

`run!` now dispatches on the model's stepper: the general method runs all `N` steps in the loop, and a method for `Simulation{<:ReactantModel{<:QuasiAdamsBashforth2TimeStepper}}` keeps the peeled forward-Euler first step and `N - 1` loop steps. AB2 is unchanged; other steppers take every step in the loop. `remainder_step!` is untouched: its `euler = true` likewise reaches only AB2.

On a 32 × 32 × 8 `HydrostaticFreeSurfaceModel` with `:SplitRungeKutta3` over 50 steps (numbers in #6329), the traced module shrinks from 167 to 94 kernel calls, the optimized module from 3,186 to 1,986 lines, and warm compile time from 4.98 s to 3.21 s, with bitwise identical fields.

The new test in `test/reactant/simulations.jl` checks, for both AB2 and `SplitRungeKutta3`, that the compiled `run!` matches the eager CPU run.

body:
Three changes that make `DateTime` (and `TimeDate`) clocks practical for forced simulations.

### `Cyclical(Year(n))` for calendar `FieldTimeSeries`

`Cyclical` with a fixed period (e.g. the inferred `Millisecond` one) drifts against the calendar by about a quarter day per year. A `Dates.Year` period instead folds the model date into the series by whole calendar years:

```julia
months = [DateTime(2018, m, 15) for m in 1:12]
climatology = FieldTimeSeries{Center, Center, Center}(grid, months; time_indexing=Cyclical(Year(1)))
climatology[1, 1, 1, Time(DateTime(1958, 3, 15))] # March
```

- Climatologies and repeat-year forcing (stamped in some nominal year) can be read at any model date, and `Cyclical(Year(61))` cycles a multi-year record.
- The wrap from the last record to the first of the next period interpolates across the real calendar gap, e.g. 31 days from 15 December to 15 January.
- Leap days follow Julia's year arithmetic: 29 February in a leap model year reads 28 February of a non-leap record.
- It works in kernels (tested through a discrete forcing on CPU; I haven't run it on a GPU).

### Numeric schedules on calendar clocks: `materialize_schedule(schedule, clock)`

A duration given as a number means seconds, just as it does for `Δt`. Before this PR, `TimeInterval(3600)` on a `DateTime` clock threw `Cannot use Float64 TimeInterval times with DateTime clock. Use a Dates.Period instead.`

The obstacle was that a schedule takes the type of its stored start time from its interval at construction, before it has seen a clock. Now `materialize_schedule(schedule, clock)` gives the schedule the clock's time type at the place where it first meets the clock:
- `JLD2Writer`, `NetCDFWriter`, `ZarrWriter` and `Checkpointer` constructors, which already called `materialize_schedule(schedule)`, except for `Checkpointer`;
- callbacks, when the simulation initializes and before a checkpoint is restored. A callback is rebuilt only when its schedule's time type changes, so schedules whose type already matches are never copied, and references to them stay valid.

This covers `TimeInterval`, `TimeOffset`, `AveragedTimeInterval`, `ConsecutiveIterations`, `OrSchedule` and `AndSchedule`. It works in both directions: `TimeInterval(Hour(1))` now also runs on a numeric clock. `AveragedTimeInterval` now advances its window with `add_time_interval` rather than raw `+`/`-`.

### `stop_time` on calendar clocks

- A `Simulation` with a `DateTime` clock and no `stop_time` threw `isless(::Float64, ::DateTime)` in `run!`. The default `Inf` now becomes the "never stop" date that `reset!` already used.
- A finite numeric `stop_time` on a calendar clock throws an `ArgumentError` at construction. `stop_time` is an instant, so it must be a date.

### Tests

`test/time_stepping/datetime_clock.jl` covers:
- climatology, repeat-year and multi-year cycles, including leap days, the December/January wrap and in-kernel use;
- numeric `TimeInterval`, `TimeOffset` and `AveragedTimeInterval` callbacks and writers on a `DateTime` clock, including checkpoint pickup;
- a `Period` schedule on a numeric clock;
- both `stop_time` cases.

Locally, `datetime_clock` (124), `simulation`, `schedules`, `output_writers`, `jld2_writer`, `checkpointer`, `averaged_specified_times`, `netcdf_writer` and `zarr_writer` all pass on CPU.

Related: #6341 (split-explicit free surface with `DateTime` clocks).

The single column `update_state!` for `HydrostaticFreeSurfaceModel` skipped several steps of the general `update_state!`. For example, a `FieldTimeSeries` forcing with an `InMemory(N)` backend never moved its in-memory window. This PR starts the single column `update_state!` with the same block as the general one: `mask_immersed_field!`, `update_model_field_time_series!`, `compute_forcing!` and `update_boundary_conditions!`.

Tests (both fail without this change):
- `time_stepping/forcings`: a single column model forced by a `FieldTimeSeries` with `backend = InMemory(2)` advances the window.
- `hydrostatic_free_surface/ensemble_models`: a single column model on an `ImmersedBoundaryGrid` matches the equivalent periodic model.
